items.q: A 66-year-old man has sudden resistance with groin pain as a stiff wire advances into the external iliac artery. Contrast hangs up in a thin parallel channel with delayed washout. Distal pulses weaken. Which wire complication does resistance with contrast hang-up in a false channel indicate?
o: Arterial dissection with an intimal flap and false lumen
Successful true-lumen wiring with expected resistance
Contrast allergy slowing the injection
Vasovagal faint affecting the wire
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Arterial dissection with an intimal flap and false lumen.** Lifted intima splits the wall into true and false channels where contrast stagnates, weakening downstream pulses.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: True lumens advance freely without pain
- C: Allergy never creates parallel channels
- D: Faints slow hearts rather than wires
**Key point:** Resistance with hang-up means dissection.
items.kp: Sudden resistance with contrast hang-up means dissection.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman has a small iliac flap seen on completion angiography with brisk preserved flow into the leg and strong pulses. The operator avoids further device passes across the flap. Which management best suits this non-flow-limiting flap with preserved pulses?
o: Observation with antiplatelets while avoiding re-crossing
Forced stenting across every visible flap
Immediate amputation for any flap
Thrombolysis into the flap plane
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Observation with antiplatelets while avoiding re-crossing.** Small flaps that preserve flow heal against the wall while extra devices risk extending the split.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Forced crossing extends dissections
- C: Amputation never treats small flaps
- D: Lysis opens flap planes further
**Key point:** Non-flow-limiting flaps heal with watching.
items.kp: Non-flow-limiting flaps heal with observation.

items.q: A 58-year-old man has a flow-limiting iliac dissection with a pale cold foot and absent pulses after catheter trauma. The true lumen is confirmed with a wire. Which endovascular tacking best restores flow in this flow-limiting flap?
o: Balloon angioplasty or stent tacking of the flap
More contrast injections to push the flap
Heating the leg with blankets alone
Waiting a year for natural healing
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Balloon angioplasty or stent tacking of the flap.** Pressing the lifted intima back against the wall with balloon or stent restores the true channel at once.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Contrast pressure extends dissections
- C: Blankets never tack intimal flaps
- D: Ischaemia cannot wait a year
**Key point:** Flow-limiting flaps need balloon or stent tacking.
r: Correct. Tack flaps with balloon or stent.
items.kp: Flow-limiting dissection flaps need balloon or stent tacking.

items.q: A 71-year-old woman has active extravasation from a torn common femoral artery with a 1 cm wall defect after a difficult large-bore stick. The leg remains viable with collateral flow. Which inside-the-artery rescue best seals this torn main lumen while preserving leg flow?
o: Covered stent bridging the defect from inside
Coil packing of the main femoral trunk
Ligation of the aorta above
Antibiotics to seal the hole
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Covered stent bridging the defect from inside.** Fabric-covered metal bridges wall holes while its lumen keeps leg blood flowing past the injury.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Trunk coils sacrifice the whole leg
- C: Aortic ligation kills both legs
- D: Antibiotics never seal arterial holes
**Key point:** Torn main lumens need covered stents.
items.kp: Torn femoral arteries need covered-stent bridging.

items.q: A 63-year-old man bleeds from a small lumbar muscular branch nicked during access, with a contained blush on angiography. The main arteries look intact and collaterals abound locally. Which branch-level rescue best suits this small bleeding side branch?
o: Coil embolisation sacrificing the small branch
Covered stent across the entire aorta
Open heart surgery for a lumbar branch
Systemic thrombolysis to stop bleeding
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Coil embolisation sacrificing the small branch.** Tiny muscular branches feed redundant networks, so coils stop the leak without meaningful tissue loss.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Aortic stents overshoot branch leaks
- C: Hearts ignore lumbar branches
- D: Lysis dissolves needed clots
**Key point:** Small branch leaks take coils.
items.kp: Bleeding muscular branches are coiled electively.

items.q: A 69-year-old woman has iliac bleeding that continues despite coils, with pressure falling and the groin balloon already inflated. The anaesthetist calls for blood while pressure holds. Which combined rescue best buys clotting time in this exsanguinating iliac injury?
o: Prolonged balloon tamponade with reversal, pressure and transfusion together
Balloon deflation to let the hole breathe
Stopping all resuscitation to save blood
Thrombolysis through the tamponade balloon
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Prolonged balloon tamponade with reversal, pressure and transfusion together.** Tamponade slows the leak while reversal, pressure and blood rebuild clotting together against shock.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Deflation restarts full bleeding
- C: Stopping resuscitation deepens shock
- D: Lysis through balloons dissolves rescue clots
**Key point:** Exsanguination needs tamponade with full resuscitation.
items.kp: Exsanguinating injuries need tamponade with full resuscitation.

items.q: A 62-year-old man has failed percutaneous closure with an expanding haematoma compressing his femoral nerve, causing foot drop. Duplex shows ongoing oozing into the confined space. Which surgical indication does this compressive neuropathy with ongoing oozing meet?
o: Surgical cutdown with evacuation and direct arterial repair
More blind pressure over the trapped nerve
Physiotherapy for the foot drop alone
Waiting months for nerve recovery
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Surgical cutdown with evacuation and direct arterial repair.** Nerve compression with active bleeding needs the haematoma released and the hole stitched under direct vision.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Blind pressure squeezes nerves further
- C: Physiotherapy never stops arterial oozing
- D: Months of waiting risks permanent palsy
**Key point:** Compressive haematomas need surgical evacuation.
r: Correct. Cut down and repair directly.
items.kp: Compressive bleeding haematomas need surgical cutdown.

items.q: A 75-year-old man develops a massively swollen tense thigh with excruciating pain after large-volume groin bleeding tamponaded late. His toes tingle and passive knee movement hurts severely. Which thigh emergency does tense swelling with stretch pain after major bleeding define?
o: Thigh compartment syndrome needing urgent fasciotomy
Simple bruising settling with ice
Muscle growth from extra blood supply
Successful tamponade with expected aching
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Thigh compartment syndrome needing urgent fasciotomy.** Blood trapped in thigh compartments crushes muscle and nerve, and only urgent surgical release saves the leg.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Bruises never tense whole thighs
- C: Blood never builds muscle
- D: Success never causes stretch agony
**Key point:** Tense thighs after bleeding mean compartments.
items.kp: Tense swollen thighs after bleeding mean compartment syndrome.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman develops blue toes with livedo rash and rising creatinine four days after rough aortoiliac catheterisation. Cholesterol crystals are suspected with normal complement levels. Which supportive strategy best manages this delayed cholesterol embolisation shower?
o: Supportive care with statins and renal protection while avoiding further catheter trauma
Emergency thrombolysis to dissolve crystals
Anticoagulation to melt cholesterol plugs
More catheterisation to flush the vessels
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Supportive care with statins and renal protection while avoiding further catheter trauma.** Crystal plugs in small vessels dissolve with nothing, so kidneys are protected while further showers are prevented.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Lysis cannot dissolve cholesterol crystals
- C: Anticoagulation never melts crystal plugs
- D: More catheters shower more crystals
**Key point:** Cholesterol showers need supportive renal care.
r: Correct. Support kidneys and stop trauma.
items.kp: Cholesterol embolisation needs supportive care with renal protection.

items.q: A 55-year-old man has a small asymptomatic groin fistula found on routine duplex two weeks after catheterisation, with normal leg swelling and no heart strain. The track measures 2 mm between tiny branches. Which natural-history plan best suits this silent small fistula?
o: Duplex watching since small silent tracks often thrombose alone
Emergency bypass surgery within the hour
High-dose steroids to close the track
Marathon running to pump it shut
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Duplex watching since small silent tracks often thrombose alone.** Tiny branch fistulae clot spontaneously within weeks, so scanning watches nature finish the job.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Bypass overshoots 2 mm branch tracks
- C: Steroids never close fistula tracks
- D: Running raises rather than seals shunts
**Key point:** Silent small fistulae merit duplex watching.
items.kp: Silent small fistulae are watched with duplex.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman has a groin shunt with marked leg swelling and ankle ulcers six weeks after catheterisation. Duplex shows a large persistent fistula with high flow. Which symptomatic threshold has this swollen ulcerated leg with high flow crossed?
o: Treatment threshold needing compression or covered-stent closure
Discharge threshold with no follow-up
Observation threshold for another decade
Antibiotic threshold for six more weeks
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Treatment threshold needing compression or covered-stent closure.** Swelling with skin breakdown proves the shunt steals meaningful flow, demanding active closure.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Discharge abandons breaking skin
- C: Decades of watching ulcerate legs fully
- D: Antibiotics never close flow shunts
**Key point:** Swollen ulcerated shunts need active closure.
items.kp: Swollen ulcerated fistulae need compression or covered stents.

items.q: A 59-year-old man has subintimal wire passage that will not re-enter the true lumen despite loop techniques. Contrast load climbs and the true channel stays elusive. Which bailout best serves this unre-enterable subintimal wire with mounting contrast?
o: Convert to another access rather than forcing onward
Force the wire until it exits the skin
Inject large contrast volumes blindly
Declare the case a success regardless
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Convert to another access rather than forcing onward.** Unre-enterable planes only extend with force while fresh access offers a clean true-lumen start.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Force exits vessels dangerously
- C: Blind volumes injure kidneys vainly
- D: False success helps nobody
**Key point:** Unre-enterable wires convert access.
items.kp: Subintimal wires that will not re-enter mean convert access.

items.q: A 67-year-old woman needs a destroyed femoral segment replaced after infection eats the wall beyond stent salvage. Surgeons plan graft material between healthy ends. Which reconstruction best bridges this unsalvageable infected arterial segment?
o: Graft interposition between healthy arterial ends
Leaving the artery discontinuous forever
Skin graft over the missing artery
Tight bandage squeezing the gap shut
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Graft interposition between healthy arterial ends.** Destroyed infected walls cannot hold stents, so a graft tube sewn between clean ends restores continuity.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Discontinuity starves the leg
- C: Skin covers rather than carries blood
- D: Bandages never bridge arterial gaps
**Key point:** Destroyed segments take graft interposition.
items.kp: Unsalvageable arterial segments need graft interposition.

items.q: A 61-year-old man returns to the ward after a bailout covered stent for iliac injury. Night observations show fresh groin swelling with a falling haemoglobin. Which post-bailout ward principle best catches this re-bleed early?
o: Joint vascular rounds with pulse, groin and haemoglobin checks
No observations after successful rescue
Discharge the same night to free beds
Forbid all blood tests after stenting
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Joint vascular rounds with pulse, groin and haemoglobin checks.** Rescued arteries can re-bleed silently, so scheduled limb and blood checks catch failure before shock.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: No watching misses re-bleeds
- C: Same-night discharge risks home collapse
- D: Banning tests blinds the team
**Key point:** Bailouts need scheduled limb and blood checks.
items.kp: Bailout rescues need joint rounds with limb and blood checks.

items.q: A 56-year-old woman asks why her small groin lump with a quiet bruit needs only scanning while her neighbour had urgent surgery. The registrar explains how symptoms sort tracks. Which exam sorting rule best separates silent from surgical tracks?
o: Watch silent small tracks while acting on symptomatic ones
Operate every lump regardless of symptoms
Scan nobody and reassure everybody
Treat neighbours identically always
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Watch silent small tracks while acting on symptomatic ones.** Symptoms mark meaningful shunts while silence marks self-sealing tracks, sorting management cleanly.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Blanket surgery overtreats widely
- C: Blanket reassurance misses danger
- D: Neighbours own different diseases
**Key point:** Symptoms sort tracks into watch versus act.
items.kp: Exam answers watch silent tracks and act on symptomatic ones.

items.q: A 60-year-old man undergoes iliac stenting and the operator shoots a completion angiogram through the sheath before closing. The image shows brisk runoff with no residual flap. The trainee asks why this final picture matters. Which safety purpose does routine completion angiography serve?
o: Mapping flaps, leaks and runoff before devices leave the table
Decorating the patient record with pictures
Increasing contrast bills for revenue
Replacing all ward observations afterwards
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Mapping flaps, leaks and runoff before devices leave the table.** Final pictures catch injuries while wires still span them, allowing instant repair before closure.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Records need function rather than decoration
- C: Contrast loads injure rather than earn
- D: Ward checks continue regardless
**Key point:** Completion angiograms catch injuries while fixable.
items.kp: Completion angiography maps injuries while still fixable.

items.q: A 57-year-old woman has a tortuous iliac segment where a stiff wire repeatedly catches side branches. The operator swaps to a soft hydrophilic wire with roadmap guidance. Which wire-selection principle best explains this swap to soft hydrophilic wires in tortuous segments?
o: Soft slippery wires negotiate bends without lifting flaps
Stiff wires straighten every tortuosity safely
Roadmaps obscure rather than guide wires
Side branches welcome stiff wire entry
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Soft slippery wires negotiate bends without lifting flaps.** Hydrophilic tips glide around bends where stiff wires spear branch mouths and lift intima.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Stiff wires spear rather than straighten
- C: Roadmaps overlay guides onto live screens
- D: Branches tear when speared
**Key point:** Tortuous segments need soft hydrophilic wires.
r: Correct. Soft wires glide around bends.
items.kp: Tortuous iliac segments need soft hydrophilic wires with roadmap.

items.q: A 65-year-old man develops a dissection while fully heparinised, with a large false channel filling. The operator debates reversing heparin immediately. Which balanced judgment best manages heparin during an active dissection with clot risk?
o: Individualise reversal since clot and bleeding risks collide
Reverse maximally in every dissection always
Give more heparin into every false channel
Ignore clotting entirely during dissections
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Individualise reversal since clot and bleeding risks collide.** False channels bleed while true lumens clot, so reversal follows the dominant danger case by case.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Blanket reversal clots true lumens
- C: More heparin feeds false channels
- D: Ignoring clotting invites thrombosis
**Key point:** Dissection heparin decisions stay individual.
items.kp: Heparin reversal during dissection is individualised.

items.q: A 62-year-old woman receives an iliac covered stent for a wall tear and asks about tablets afterwards. The team prescribes antiplatelets to keep the stent open. Which post-stent drug principle best explains antiplatelets after covered metal?
o: Metal in blood needs platelet quieting to prevent in-stent clots
Stents dissolve without daily tablets
Antiplatelets melt the metal coating
Tablets replace all follow-up scans
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Metal in blood needs platelet quieting to prevent in-stent clots.** Fresh metal invites platelet clumps until endothelium covers it, so quiet platelets keep rescue stents open.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Metal persists rather than dissolving
- C: Drugs never melt stent fabric
- D: Scans continue alongside tablets
**Key point:** Covered stents need antiplatelets against clots.
r: Correct. Quiet platelets keep stents open.
items.kp: Rescue stents need antiplatelets until endothelialised.

items.q: A 54-year-old man has a tacked iliac flap with restored pulses and goes home. The team books duplex at one month with pulse checks. Which follow-up principle best justifies scheduled duplex after tacked dissections?
o: Confirming lasting patency and catching silent re-narrowing
Duplex heals flaps with sound waves
Follow-up replaces the need for tablets
One scan cures all future disease
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Confirming lasting patency and catching silent re-narrowing.** Tacked flaps can scar down silently, so timed duplex proves flow lasts and triggers re-treatment early.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Sound waves image rather than heal
- C: Tablets continue alongside scans
- D: Arteries need lifelong watching
**Key point:** Tacked flaps need timed duplex proof.
items.kp: Tacked dissections need scheduled duplex follow-up.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman bleeds briskly from groin access with pressure falling despite tamponade. Bloods show haemoglobin 62 g/L with coagulopathy developing. Which transfusion trigger best suits this exsanguinating access bleed with coagulopathy?
o: Transfuse early with blood products as shock with coagulopathy demands
Withhold all blood until morning rounds
Transfuse only after full cardiac arrest
Give water by mouth instead of blood
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Transfuse early with blood products as shock with coagulopathy demands.** Exsanguination with failing clotting kills quickly, so blood with clotting factors starts during tamponade.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Morning rounds arrive after death
- C: Arrest resuscitation starts too late
- D: Water never carries oxygen
**Key point:** Exsanguination transfuses early with products.
items.kp: Exsanguinating access bleeds transfuse early with blood products.

items.q: A 59-year-old man has groin oozing with oozing from gums and venepuncture sites during a long heparinised case. The team considers an antifibrinolytic alongside pressure. Which adjunct role best describes tranexamic acid in bleeding access cases?
o: Antifibrinolytic adjunct that steadies clots alongside pressure
Clot dissolver that clears the field
Substitute for all surgical repair
Antibiotic preventing wound infection
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Antifibrinolytic adjunct that steadies clots alongside pressure.** Tranexamic acid slows clot breakdown while pressure and repair stop the leak itself.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Dissolvers oppose the goal directly
- C: Drugs never replace torn walls
- D: Antibiotics never steady clots
**Key point:** Tranexamic steadies clots beside pressure.
items.kp: Tranexamic acid adjuncts pressure in bleeding access.

items.q: A 33-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks needs urgent bleeding embolisation and worries about groin complications harming her pregnancy. The team picks ultrasound-guided micropuncture with minimal screening. Which pregnancy-adapted access principle best protects mother and fetus?
o: Lowest-dose ultrasound-first access with abdominal shielding
Avoiding all treatment until delivery regardless
Maximum radiation for the clearest pictures
Femoral cutdown under no anaesthesia
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Lowest-dose ultrasound-first access with abdominal shielding.** Ultrasound sticks need no X-rays while shielding and pulsed screening minimise fetal dose during treatment.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Delaying lets bleeding kill both
- C: Maximum dose harms fetuses needlessly
- D: Cutdowns still need anaesthesia
**Key point:** Pregnancy access minimises fetal dose.
items.kp: Pregnant access uses ultrasound-first technique with shielding.

items.q: A 70-year-old man consents for femoral angioplasty and asks what could go wrong with the groin. The operator lists bleeding, clots, false sacs and rescue surgery. Which consent standard does this frank groin-risk discussion meet?
o: Montgomery material-risk disclosure of what a reasonable patient would want to know
No disclosure needed for routine groins
Listing only benefits without any risks
Asking relatives instead of the patient
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Montgomery material-risk disclosure of what a reasonable patient would want to know.** UK Montgomery consent requires sharing risks a reasonable patient would weigh, including groin rescue surgery.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Routine groins still carry material risks
- C: Benefits-only consent misleads
- D: Patients themselves must be told
**Key point:** Groin consent follows Montgomery disclosure.
items.kp: Access consent discloses material groin risks per Montgomery.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman has her access details recorded with sheath size, closure method and pedal pulses after the case. The night team reads the note and checks the groin confidently. Which documentation standard best explains this useful access note?
o: Complete access records let night teams watch the right risks
Notes exist only for legal decoration
Pulse records never change management
Night teams should guess access details
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Complete access records let night teams watch the right risks.** Sheath size, closure and pulses tell the night team what to check and when to escalate.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Notes actively guide night care
- C: Pulse losses trigger rescue directly
- D: Guessing misses re-bleeds
**Key point:** Access notes direct night watching.
items.kp: Complete access documentation directs night-team watching.
